old: - Benjamin CL, et al. Physiological Responses to Heat Acclimation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2019. PMID 31191102.
new: - Rahimi GRM, Albanaqi AL, Van der Touw T, et al. Physiological Responses to Heat Acclimation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2019;18(2):316–326. PMID 31191102.
note: Wrong first author: PMID 31191102 is by Rahimi GRM, Albanaqi AL, Van der Touw T et al., J Sports Sci Med 2019;18:316-326 (checked via NCBI E-utilities). 'Benjamin CL' is not an author.
Internal inconsistency: the test is 30 min; sweat rate 1.1-1.3 L/h gives ~0.55-0.65 kg loss, which is 1.6-1.8% only for a ~35 kg athlete. ~0.8-1.0% fits a ~65 kg adult.

old: - Stopping sweating, or hot, dry skin
new: - Hot skin, whether dry or still sweating (many exertional heatstroke casualties are still sweating)
note: Safety: in exertional heatstroke the skin is often still wet; 'stopped sweating/dry skin' as a criterion delays recognition. ACSM Expert Consensus on Exertional Heat Illness (Roberts et al., Curr Sports Med Rep 2021;20(9):470-484); NATA position statement (Casa et al., J Athl Train 2015).

old: Rapid cooling and emergency care save lives.
new: Rapid whole-body cooling, ideally cold-water immersion started on site as soon as heatstroke is suspected, and emergency care save lives.
note: Safety: consensus is 'cool first, transport second' with cold-water immersion as the gold standard (Roberts et al. 2021 ACSM consensus; Casa et al. 2015 NATA). Current text does not say how to cool.

old: |Above 28°C|Very high|Consider postponing or moving hard sessions; follow medical guidance|
new: |Above 28°C|Extreme|Postpone, cancel or move sessions indoors; follow medical guidance|
note: ACSM 2007 position stand (Armstrong et al., MSSE 39:556-572) treats WBGT >28°C as extreme/black flag: cancel continuous activity/races. 'Consider postponing hard sessions' understates the risk.

old: ask for haemoglobin and ferritin at least twice a year, and before and after any altitude block. It is cheap
new: ask a doctor to arrange haemoglobin and ferritin testing at least twice a year and before and after any altitude block, and let the clinician interpret the results. It is cheap
note: Contradicts the book's own rules (Ch. 45 'question first, clinician interprets'; Ch. 81 rule 4) by having the coach order/interpret blood tests. Ferritin rises with inflammation and needs clinical reading.

old: found anaemia in 44% of adolescent girls and 41% of adult women. A 2025 study
new: found anaemia in 44% of adolescent girls and 41% of adult women, although iron deficiency explained less than a third of it. A 2025 study
note: The cited survey (Ghosh et al., Eur J Clin Nutr 2025;79:443-451, PMID 39779946) concludes iron-deficiency anaemia was <1/3 of anaemia; 'other' causes predominated. Without this the hypothesis over-links anaemia to iron.

old: - Anaemia prevalence across eight Indian states (venous blood survey). PubMed. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39779946/
new: - Ghosh S, Laxmaiah A, Chandak GR, et al. Anaemia and iron deficiency in India: a venous blood-based survey of adolescents, adults, and the elderly in eight states. European Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 2025;79(5):443–451. PMID 39779946.
note: Incomplete citation; full details verified via NCBI E-utilities for PMID 39779946.

old: - Jegatheesan SL, et al. Hematological status, dietary iron intake and endurance in Indian female athletes. Physical Activity and Nutrition. 2025. PMID 40443248.
new: - Jegatheesan SL, Kumbamoorthy SS, Sanjaykumar S, Rajkumar NCJ. Unlocking the connection: hematological status, dietary iron intake and endurance in Indian female athletes. Physical Activity and Nutrition. 2025;29(1):31–37. PMID 40443248.
note: Title truncated; full title/volume verified via NCBI (PMID 40443248). Data in text (104 volleyball/ball-badminton players, 53.8% anaemic) match the abstract.
Add volume/pages (verified NCBI PMID 38051495, Brown HA, Topham TH, Clark B et al.).

new: - Solomon TPJ, Laye MJ. The effect
note: Use standard author format (PMID 39762944: Solomon TPJ, Laye MJ; BMC Sports Sci Med Rehabil 2025;17:4).

old: who will watch for early signs of heat illness such as confusion
new: who will watch for signs of serious heat illness such as confusion
note: Confusion, collapse and unsteady running are signs of heatstroke (CNS dysfunction), not early signs; calling them 'early' could delay action.

old: stops sweating or develops hot, dry skin, collapses
new: has hot skin (dry or still sweating), collapses
note: Same heatstroke-recognition issue as Ch. 81 list: sweating often persists in exertional heatstroke (ACSM 2021 consensus).

old: across 42 kilometres it is roughly three and a half minutes
new: across 42 kilometres it is roughly three minutes
note: Arithmetic: Rio 2:15:25 (3:12.6/km) to Valencia 2:12:23 (3:08.2/km) = 4.4 s/km, i.e. 3:02 over the marathon, not ~3.5 min.

old: A 2% improvement in running economy means nothing if the test's typical error is 3%.
new: A 2% improvement in running economy cannot be distinguished from noise if the test's typical error is 3%.
note: Overstated: a change smaller than typical error is uncertain, not meaningless (Hopkins 2000; Hopkins et al. 2009).

new: |Above 28|Move indoors or rest; outdoors only short, very easy and supervised|Postpone|
note: Align with ACSM black-flag guidance (>28°C WBGT: cancel continuous outdoor exercise) and Ch. 51 table.

old: These are known technical limitations of optical sensing
new: These are recognised potential limitations of optical sensing, although the evidence on skin tone is mixed
note: Bent et al., npj Digit Med 2020;3:18 found no significant accuracy difference by skin tone, while other studies report errors; motion/intensity effects are better established.
